I've completed the research across official university sources. Here's the comparison.

---

# Master's in Computer Science in Germany — Comparison for International Students

**Method note:** All figures below come from official university pages (tum.de, rwth-aachen.de, uni-saarland.de, tu-darmstadt.de, kit.edu, informatik.uni-bonn.de). Where a Google AI summary conflicted with an official page, I went to the official source — e.g. the AI summary gave Saarland's fee as €412.30 while a university page listed "€111.30–€156.30"; the official breakdown resolved this: €412.30 total, of which €226.80 is the nationwide transit ticket and the smaller figure is only the student-services portion. No applications were submitted and no login was used.

## The single biggest differentiator: tuition is *not* uniform

The "study in Germany for free" assumption is now outdated in two of these states.

| University | Tuition (non-EU/EEA) | Semester fee | Language | Admission gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **TUM** (Garching/Munich) | **€4,000–6,000 / semester** | €97 | English | Aptitude Assessment (points → possible interview) |
| **RWTH Aachen** | None (NRW) | ~€300–380 | **German *and* English** | Open (no NC) |
| **Saarland** (Saarbrücken) | None | €412.30 | English only | No NC, but motivation letter + 2 references |
| **TU Darmstadt** | None (Hesse) | ~€290–380 | English | No NC, but possible **on-campus written exam** |
| **KIT** (Karlsruhe) | **€1,500 / semester** + €80 admin + €92 services | included above | **German C1** | Capacity-limited + strict ECTS thresholds |
| **Bonn** | None (NRW) | ~€350 | English (no German needed) | Selective; strict prior-knowledge check |

Over a 2-year degree, TUM costs roughly **€16,000–24,000** in tuition; KIT about **€6,000**; Aachen, Saarbrücken, Darmstadt and Bonn essentially **€0**. KIT lists exemptions (EU/EEA citizens, German Abitur holders, exchange students, PhD students, certain BW-Stiftung scholarship holders).

## Program-by-program findings

**TUM — M.Sc. Informatics.** Four semesters, 120 ECTS, English, available full-time *or* part-time, entry in both winter and summer. Application windows: 1 Feb–31 May (winter), 1 Oct–30 Nov (summer). Admission runs through the Aptitude Assessment: grades and written documents are scored on a point system; applicants who earned their bachelor's outside the Lisbon Convention area may have to sit an **online test**; borderline candidates get a 20-minute interview, which TUM confirms is commonly done by phone or video for international applicants. A useful provision: Bavarian law allows a "soft transition" — you may enroll before your final bachelor's certificate is issued, submitting it within a year.

**RWTH Aachen — M.Sc. Computer Science.** Four semesters, 120 ECTS, both intakes, and notably **open admission with no NC**. The catch is language: the program is delivered in German *and* English and expects proficiency in **both**. This is the most common reason candidates rule it out despite the easy formal admission.

**Saarland — M.Sc. Computer Science.** Fully English, four semesters, not admission-restricted. Two important practical details: the C1 English requirement **explicitly does not accept a Medium-of-Instruction certificate** (a frequent tripwire for South Asian applicants who assume their English-taught bachelor's suffices), and the application needs a motivation letter plus **two academic references** — so line up referees early. Its research draw is unusual for a mid-sized university: the Saarland Informatics Campus co-locates two Max Planck Institutes (Informatics; Software Systems), the CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, and DFKI.

**TU Darmstadt — M.Sc. Computer Science.** English, with specialization tracks including Data Science & Engineering, Visual Computing and Distributed Computing. Two things worth flagging: the separate M.Sc. Distributed Software Systems has been **discontinued**, so older guides pointing there are stale; and while there's no NC, applicants whose "entrance competencies" can't be verified from the transcript may be required to sit a **90-minute written entrance exam on campus in Darmstadt** — a serious logistical and cost barrier from abroad. GRE or GATE scores can qualify you for a waiver, which is the practical workaround. You may also apply for only **one** program per admission period across their related CS master's.

**KIT — M.Sc. Informatics.** The flagship program is **taught in German and requires C1 German regardless of citizenship**, proven by end of enrollment at the latest. It also sets the most explicit prerequisites of any school here: 15 CP theoretical CS, 30 CP practical CS, 8 CP computer engineering, 25 CP mathematics. Miss those and you can still qualify via an **aptitude interview** (possible over Zoom) against slightly lower thresholds (15/20/6/20). Deadlines are 15 July (winter) and 15 January (summer). KIT announced new English-taught master's programs in 2025, so if you like Karlsruhe but lack German, that's the thread to pull.

**Bonn — M.Sc. Computer Science** (alongside AI, Cyber Security and Mobile Robotics). English C1, **no German required**. Bonn is exceptionally transparent about selectivity, and one line on its official admissions page deserves direct quotation: *"More than 99 percent of applicants from these countries are rejected because the curricula of their degree programs or their theses do not meet our requirements"* — referring to bachelor's degrees from **Bangladesh, India, Nepal, Pakistan or Afghanistan**. Bonn also warns that its application portal cannot tell you which deadline applies to you, so verify against the deadlines page before submitting.

## Cross-cutting rules that apply wherever you go

- **Blocked account:** €11,904 per year (€992/month) for 2026, deposited before your visa appointment.
- **Working during studies:** 140 full days or 280 half days per year.
- **After graduation:** an 18-month job-seeking residence permit, during which hour limits disappear entirely — you can work full-time in any job while searching, then convert to a work visa or EU Blue Card. Apply before your student permit expires.
- **Visa timing:** Bonn explicitly advises booking a visa appointment as early as possible, since only a few months separate admission from semester start in many countries.

## How I'd read this

If **cost dominates**, Saarland, Darmstadt, Aachen and Bonn are effectively free, and TUM's €4,000–6,000 per semester is a real six-semester-equivalent expense that rankings won't tell you about.

If you **don't speak German**, KIT's main program and RWTH are effectively closed regardless of your profile — this filters more candidates than any GPA cutoff.

If your **bachelor's is from South Asia**, take Bonn's 99% figure seriously and weight Saarland and Darmstadt higher, but budget for GRE/GATE to sidestep Darmstadt's on-campus exam, and get a real C1 English certificate rather than an MOI letter for Saarland.

If **research access** is the goal, Saarbrücken's concentration of two Max Planck Institutes plus CISPA is disproportionate to the city's size, and it happens to be among the cheapest places on this list to live.

Two caveats: fees and deadlines are revised annually — reconfirm on the official pages in the term you apply. I'd also verify Saarland's exact application dates directly, as their "at a glance" table lists an early and a late round whose mapping to winter/summer intake I'd want you to read first-hand before diarizing.
